heart_rate.label: Heart rate

input.help: Resting heart rate, in beats per minute.
input.note: Plausibility limit for data entry, not a medical threshold.

heart_rate.why_in_space: Weightlessness changes blood circulation and how the heart and blood vessels work. NASA's Human Research Program studies these cardiovascular adaptations.

guidance.normal: Nothing to do. Keep your regular measurement schedule.
guidance.attention: Measure again at rest. The American Heart Association suggests checking resting heart rate first thing in the morning, before getting up. Above 100 bpm at rest is outside the normal range (AHA): if it stays there, mention it to your flight surgeon at your next check-in.
guidance.critical: Heart rate has no emergency threshold in this prototype. If you feel unwell, contact your flight surgeon.

autonomy_steps: Rest for 5 minutes, then measure your heart rate again to confirm the reading.
Check related indicators now: blood pressure and body temperature.
Notify the Crew Medical Officer on board.
Open the onboard medical procedure for a fast resting heart rate.
Log any symptoms (palpitations, dizziness, shortness of breath) with the time.

bp_systolic.label: Blood pressure (systolic)

input.help: Top number of your blood pressure reading.
input.note: Plausibility limit for data entry, not a medical threshold.

bp_systolic.what: Pressure in the arteries when the heart contracts.
bp_systolic.why_in_space: Part of the cardiovascular picture NASA monitors during spaceflight.

guidance.normal: Nothing to do. Keep your regular measurement schedule.
guidance.attention: Sit still for a few minutes and measure again. Low blood pressure without symptoms is often harmless (NHLBI); tell your flight surgeon if you feel dizzy or faint.
guidance.critical: The American Heart Association advises waiting five minutes and measuring again. If it is still outside the range, contact your flight surgeon now.

autonomy_steps: Sit still for 5 minutes, then measure your blood pressure again to confirm the reading.
Check related indicators now: heart rate and body temperature.
Notify the Crew Medical Officer on board.
Open the onboard medical procedure for high or low blood pressure.
Log any symptoms (headache, dizziness, vision changes) with the time.

bp_diastolic.label: Blood pressure (diastolic)

input.help: Bottom number of your blood pressure reading.
input.note: Plausibility limit for data entry, not a medical threshold.

bp_diastolic.what: Pressure in the arteries between two heartbeats.
bp_diastolic.why_in_space: Part of the cardiovascular picture NASA monitors during spaceflight.

guidance.normal: Nothing to do. Keep your regular measurement schedule.
guidance.attention: Sit still for a few minutes and measure again. Low blood pressure without symptoms is often harmless (NHLBI); tell your flight surgeon if you feel dizzy or faint.
guidance.critical: The American Heart Association advises waiting five minutes and measuring again. If it is still outside the range, contact your flight surgeon now.

autonomy_steps: Sit still for 5 minutes, then measure your blood pressure again to confirm the reading.
Check related indicators now: heart rate and body temperature.
Notify the Crew Medical Officer on board.
Open the onboard medical procedure for high or low blood pressure.
Log any symptoms (headache, dizziness, vision changes) with the time.

glucose.label: Blood glucose

input.note: Plausibility limit for data entry, not a medical threshold.

glucose.what: Amount of sugar in the blood.
glucose.why_in_space: A balanced diet is essential on long missions. NASA lists inadequate food and nutrition as a spaceflight risk.

guidance.normal: Nothing to do. Keep your regular measurement schedule.
guidance.attention: Note when you last ate and measure again later. If it stays above 240 mg/dL (ADA), tell your flight surgeon.
guidance.critical: This value is outside the range set by American Diabetes Association guidance. Measure again, then contact your flight surgeon now.

autonomy_steps: Measure your blood glucose again in 15 minutes to confirm the reading.
Check related indicators now: heart rate, body temperature and mood.
Notify the Crew Medical Officer on board.
Open the onboard medical procedure for high or low blood glucose.
Log any symptoms (shakiness, confusion, thirst) and the time of your last meal.

temperature.label: Body temperature

input.note: Plausibility limit for data entry, not a medical threshold.

temperature.why_in_space: The stress of spaceflight can alter immune responses and reactivate dormant viruses (NASA Human Research Program).

guidance.normal: Nothing to do. Keep your regular measurement schedule.
guidance.attention: Measure again in an hour and note any symptoms (rash, cough, chills).
guidance.critical: 38 °C or more is a fever by the CDC definition; below 35 °C is an emergency. Contact your flight surgeon now and note any symptoms.

autonomy_steps: Measure your temperature again in 15 minutes to confirm the reading.
Check related indicators now: heart rate and blood pressure.
Notify the Crew Medical Officer on board.
Open the onboard medical procedure for fever or low body temperature.
Log any symptoms (chills, cough, fatigue) with the time.

sleep_hours.label: Sleep

input.help: Hours slept in the last 24 h. 7.5 = 7 h 30 min.
input.note: Plausibility limit for data entry, not a medical threshold.

sleep_hours.what: Hours of sleep over the last 24 hours.
sleep_hours.why_in_space: NASA lists inadequate sleep and irregular schedules among the risks of long missions: they affect alertness, mood and performance.

guidance.normal: Nothing to do. Keep protecting your rest window.
guidance.attention: Adults need at least 7 hours of sleep (AASM, CDC). Keep regular sleep and wake times, and put screens away before rest. If it stays low, raise it at the next comm pass.

mood.label: Mood (self-reported)

input.help: How do you feel right now?
input.note: Plausibility limit for data entry, not a medical threshold.

mood.what: Self-assessment from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good). Not a clinical scale.
mood.why_in_space: Isolation, confinement and distance from Earth can take a toll on mental health. NASA tracks this as a behavioral health risk.

guidance.normal: Nothing to do. Keep checking in daily.
guidance.attention: Write a short note on how you feel. NASA tracks behavioral health as a spaceflight risk: talking with the crew or the support team on Earth is part of the routine, not an exception.
